_notes: T2.108 -- the G-C measurement corpus. Content first, origins second.
T2.129 grew it past the false-promotion audit's decidability band and
armed the audit's machine arm; the design rules below are unchanged and
were not relaxed to reach the count.
Every entry is a capture that a working agent could plausibly have made,
and the corroboration structure is a property of WHO captured WHAT and
WHEN, never of a per-memory unique origin_key. Echo is not evidence: the
`echo` group below states one claim three times from ONE capture session
and is expected never to promote, and the `under_sourced` group states one
claim from two same-week sessions of the same kind, which is k=2 against
N=3. Both are results, not defects.
Seven groups. Three target a different threshold gate, two are the
designed refusals, the sixth is T2.129's arming pair, and the seventh is
T2.129's blocked-hold chain:
diversity  -- project `default`. A payments service whose dependency set
is recorded in memory by the agents working on it AND
independently asserted by the indexed repository's own
parsed imports (repo_fixture.json). Two attributable
origins of two kinds (`memory`, `code`) is the diversity
gate, N=2. This is doc 10 6's designed bridge, not a
contrivance: the parse and the human note are genuinely
independent witnesses of the same dependency. Grown from 11
claims to 80 by giving the service the dependency set a real
one of its size has, and by spreading the notes over six
capture sessions rather than one.
time_gap   -- project `atlas`. A data platform whose operational facts
were recorded once and independently re-recorded by a later
session at least seven days on. Two attributable origins
>= 7 days apart is N=2. Grown from 10 claims to 18.
none       -- project `ledger`. Three same-week sessions of the same
kind: no gate fires, so the default N=3 applies and is met
by the count alone. Grown from 10 claims to 32.
echo       -- project `ledger`. ONE session saving one claim three times.
One origin however many rows: stays `candidate`.
under_sourced -- project `ledger`. Two same-kind sessions inside one week:
k=2 against N=3, so it stays `candidate`.
armed_subject / armed_counterpart -- project `warehouse`, which nothing
else uses. Three same-week sessions record that trino
replaced hive (N=3 by count, so it promotes on both passes
including the unsimulated one). A later session re-confirms
it -- that re-assertion is what puts the fact back in front
of the recompute's fast arm -- and an independent session
records the rollback, hive replacing trino. That inverse
REPLACES pair is what arms `inverse_replacement`, judge-free
and with no dependency on G-D. The rollback session's origin
appears nowhere in the subject claim, because the veto's
echo test asks whether the counterpart brings a witness the
subject does not have.
blocked_hold -- project `scheduler`, which nothing else uses. Three
sessions inside one week record that dagster replaced
oozie, deliberately dated INSIDE the 90-day supersession
window (`now-<N>d`, resolved against the run clock at
load): ingest retires each capture under the next, and the
ladder journals a `supersession_blocked` hold on a fact
that met its count -- the other arm the 2026-08-13 owner
ruling requires to fire in a measured window, and the one
the arming groups' window clause forecloses there. This is
also the one group whose database state is reachable
through a capture door: production stamps created_at at
ingest, so three same-claim captures days apart cannot all
survive `active`. Expected to hold at `candidate` forever;
a promotion here means the hold failed.
`wave` is which ingestion pass an entry belongs to and defaults to 1. The
arming pair's wave-2 entries arrive AFTER the corpus's first recompute has
converged, because the audit's numerator counts a fact corroborated and
THEN disputed: a counterpart present from the start would send the fact
candidate -> disputed with no corroboration in between, and the numerator
would stay 0 with the arm armed -- a vacuum one layer down.
EDITING CONSTRAINT: the corroboration structure is validated by
promotion_corpus.validate_corroboration_design, validate_arming_design
and validate_blocked_hold_design. Adding an origin, moving a date across
the seven-day gap, moving an arming entry between waves, dating an arming
entry inside the supersession window, or dating a blocked_hold entry
outside it (or absolutely at all) changes what a group demonstrates, and
each is refused rather than silently honoured.
T2.131 grew the corpus to the window that settles the audit. T2.132 moved
the false-promotion audit onto the 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound, and at
this corpus's k = 1 that bound needs a window near 500 rather than the 149
T2.129 reached: 490 is the floor and the growth is sized to an expected 500,
because a floor is not a target. 377 new claims at the adjudicated split --
264 `diversity` and 113 `none` -- for +603 captures. The design rules below
are unchanged and none was relaxed to reach the count.
The two arms grew for different reasons and cost different amounts.
`diversity` converts near one for one and is therefore the cheap arm, but it
could not grow inside one repository: the validator refuses two claims naming
one dependency, deliberately, and the original repo was claim-saturated. So
repo_fixture.json became a fleet of six and each claim now names its repo as
well as its dependency. Those claims CANNOT leave project `default` --
fact_lift.CODE_FACT_PROJECT is that constant and `repositories` carries no
project -- so a diversity claim authored elsewhere would lift to a fact the
repository never seconds and would hold at one origin with no error. That is
a disclosed confinement, not an oversight: `default` holds 365 of the 529
promoting claims.
`none` costs three captures per claim and is the ONLY arm that can spread
across projects, so the 113 new claims are spread over five new ones --
signal, harbor, foundry, orchard and basalt, three services each. They are
new rather than added to `ledger` so that no growth capture can re-assert a
control claim's triple: `claim_key` groups by key and not by content, so a
differently-keyed capture asserting the echo claim's content in `ledger`
would add an origin and promote a designed refusal, and no validator refuses
it.
NO GROWTH CAPTURE CARRIES REPLACEMENT LANGUAGE. A REPLACES-family edge
cannot move `k` in any corpus this loader admits, so this is hygiene rather
than a k-guard -- but detect_supersessions is same-project and the `none`
arm is three captures asserting one claim inside one week, which is exactly
the shape that retired pass 1's arming captures under each other and made
supersession_hold withhold the promotion. Nothing inspects extractor
emissions, so there is no authoring-time catch and the rule is the catch.
The growth is also dated before the supersession look-back window, which is
a monotone property: a date outside the window never re-enters it.

orchard-media uses seaweedfs as the object store the renditions land in.
orchard-media uses seaweedfs. Volumes are replicated across two racks.

orchard-media uses temporal to run a transcode as a durable workflow.
orchard-media uses temporal. A failed transcode resumes from its last completed step.

orchard-media uses nats to carry transcode jobs to the workers.
orchard-media uses nats. Workers acknowledge a job before starting.

orchard-media uses exiftool. Stripping happens before the asset is stored.

orchard-cdn uses haproxy to balance across the origin replicas.
orchard-cdn uses haproxy. Health checks run against the rendition endpoint.

orchard-cdn uses bunny as the public delivery network.
orchard-cdn uses bunny. Signed URLs expire after fifteen minutes.

orchard-cdn uses wireguard for the link between the edge and the origin.
orchard-cdn uses wireguard. Keys rotate on a monthly cycle.

orchard-cdn uses coredns to resolve the edge hostnames internally.
orchard-cdn uses coredns. Split horizon keeps internal traffic off the public path.
Confirmed during the network review that orchard-cdn uses coredns.
orchard-cdn uses goaccess to summarise the edge access logs.
orchard-cdn uses goaccess. The summary feeds the weekly delivery report.

orchard-cdn uses victoriametrics for the edge hit ratio metric.
orchard-cdn uses victoriametrics. The ratio is reported per region.

orchard-index uses opensearch for the asset search index.
orchard-index uses opensearch. The index carries the rights window on every document.

orchard-index uses qdrant for the visual similarity search.
orchard-index uses qdrant. Vectors are produced at ingest and never at query time.

orchard-index uses scylla to hold the per-asset view counters.
orchard-index uses scylla. Counters are written asynchronously.

orchard-index uses flink. The job checkpoints every thirty seconds.

orchard-index uses redpanda as the event log the view events land on.
orchard-index uses redpanda. Retention is seven days.

orchard-index uses airflow to run the nightly rights reconciliation.

orchard-index uses duckdb for the analyst queries over the exported view data.

orchard-index uses minio to hold the exported analytics files.

basalt-router uses osrm to compute a driving route between two stops.

basalt-router uses valhalla for the routes that need turn restrictions.
basalt-router uses valhalla. It runs on its own tile set.

basalt-router uses h3 to bucket stops into cells before planning.
basalt-router uses h3. Resolution nine is what the planner assumes.

basalt-router uses ortools to solve the vehicle assignment.

basalt-router uses postgis for the geometry the planner reads.

basalt-router uses temporal to run a plan as a durable workflow.

basalt-router uses nats to publish a completed plan to the dispatch side.

basalt-fleet uses emqx as the broker the vehicle telemetry arrives on.

basalt-fleet uses timescaledb for the vehicle position history.

basalt-fleet uses questdb for the high rate sensor series.
basalt-fleet uses questdb. The series are queried by the maintenance team only.

basalt-fleet uses grafana for the depot operations dashboards.
basalt-fleet uses grafana. Dashboards are provisioned per depot.

basalt-fleet uses keycloak for the dispatcher sign-in.

basalt-fleet uses wireguard for the link from the depot to the platform.
basalt-fleet uses wireguard. Each depot has its own key pair.

basalt-fleet uses cilium for the network policy between the fleet services.

basalt-geocoder uses libpostal to normalise an address before geocoding.

basalt-geocoder uses opensearch for the address autocomplete in the dispatcher console.

basalt-geocoder uses minio to hold the generated tile sets.

basalt-geocoder uses duckdb for the analyst queries over the geocoding outcomes.
